provider: NCBI SRA — with anonymous read via AWS Open Data

free_tier.stated: No per-account quota published. Submission is genuinely bulk: FTP, Aspera (`ascp -QT -l 100m -k1 -d`), or Aspermera; operator guidance for 'tens or more terabytes' is to contact SRA support directly.
free_tier.notes: Headline offer; binding constraint specified in limits.

per_object_cap.stated: No per-object cap documented in published terms; absence is not an unlimited claim.
per_object_cap.notes: extraction found no per-object clause; some of these providers meter on object count rather than bytes, and some state no cap

retention.stated: per-object-cap: none on deposit; individual runs of hundreds of GB are normal. Retention: permanent, no expiry

egress.terms: Free. Read side is mirrored to AWS Open Data (`sra-pub-run-odp.s3.amazonaws.com`) with anonymous, ranged, CORS-open access. No requester-pays, no auth.

tooling: Aspera Connect / ascp, sra-tools (prefetch/fasterq-dump), and the AWS Open Data mirror which behaves like any public S3 bucket.
chaining: Deposit is per-submission and effectively unbounded; the AWS mirror means the fetch workload does not touch NCBI's own edge at all, so read capacity is Amazon's, not NCBI's. Each public run is an independently addressable anonymous object.
limits_note: Per-object-cap: none on deposit; individual runs of hundreds of GB are normal. Retention: permanent, no expiry. Binding limit on read is per-ip-shaping from S3. Not a storage cap.
reliability_note: Historically flaky FTP uploads ('frequent drop-outs, you only have a few minutes from logging in'); Aspera is the working path. Anonymous S3 mirror can lag NCBI's own copy.
confidence_note: Unverified: carried from historical research records without live verification. A first-party page read confirms documentation.
